channel.title: KhingBoard
channel.description: Update feed for KhingBoard, the macOS whiteboard for AI context.

item.description:
You can now choose KhingBoard from a board file's Open With menu.

Fixed

  • KhingBoard was missing from Open With for .excalidraw files. It deliberately does not take the association away from Excalidraw or your browser, but it was declaring that a shade too strongly — strongly enough that macOS left it out of the list altogether, so double-clicking a board reached TextEdit and there was no way to point it at KhingBoard by hand. It is now offered alongside the others, and Always Open With sticks if you pick it.

Nothing else changed from 0.2.

A real editor around the canvas: properties, layers, groups, and a crash fixed.

Fixed

  • KhingBoard could quit while saving. A background save called into the document from the wrong thread and tripped a Swift concurrency check, which ends the app outright rather than raising anything you could dismiss. It could happen on any save, including the automatic ones, so this is the reason to update even if nothing below appeals.

New

  • A Properties panel. Everything about the selected shape in one place: position and size, rotation, corner rounding, stroke colour, width, style and sloppiness, fill and fill style, opacity, and the full type controls — font, size, line height, and both alignments. With nothing selected it edits the defaults instead, so you can set up how the next thing you draw will look.
  • A Layers panel. Every element on the board, front to back, with frames and their contents nested underneath. Click to select, drag to reorder, drag onto a frame to move something into it, and lock anything you want to stop hitting by accident. Double-click a frame's row to rename it.
  • Group and ungroup, on ⌘G and ⇧⌘G. Clicking one member takes the whole group; the Layers panel is how you reach a single element inside one. Groups are written into the file the way Excalidraw writes them, so a grouped board opens grouped there too.
  • An image tool. Press I or use the last button on the tool bar, choose a file, and click to place it. Images could previously only arrive by dragging or pasting them in.
  • A right-click menu on the canvas, with cut, copy, paste, delete, group, the arrange commands and lock. Paste and Insert Image… land where you clicked.
  • Align, distribute and flip, plus arrowheads you can change after the fact on either end of an arrow.
  • Figma's keyboard shortcuts for the tools: V H R O D A L P T S F, and I for images. The arrow is A rather than Figma's ⇧L, because on a whiteboard the arrow is the mark you reach for constantly.

Better

  • A new app icon, the Markup Arrow, on the app, the menu bar and your board files alike.
  • A menu bar item, for a new board, your recent ones, and checking for updates without going hunting for the window.
  • A redesigned start page, with a picture of each recent board rather than just its name, and when you last touched it.
  • Boards open at a usable size. New windows were opening small enough that the panels crowded the canvas.
  • Tooltips on the tool bar and the zoom controls, each with its shortcut.

Sketch the thing, then hand the whole board to your AI.

New

  • An infinite canvas built for briefing a model. Boxes, arrows, text, sticky notes and dropped images on a space that never runs out. Arrows stay attached to the shapes they connect, so moving a box redraws the flow instead of stranding the line.
  • Copy as AI context, on ⇧⌘C. One shortcut puts two things on the clipboard at once: a picture of the board, and a written description of it. Paste into Claude, ChatGPT or anything else and both arrive together. The picture carries the layout, the text carries the exact labels and which arrow joins what, so nothing rests on the model squinting at your handwriting.
  • Reads and writes .excalidraw files. Boards are plain files in a format other tools already open, kept where you put them. Nothing is locked in a library, and opening a board someone sent you works.
  • Agents can read the board themselves. KhingBoard runs a local MCP server with a get_board tool, so Claude Code can look at what you have drawn without an export-and-paste round trip. Sketch, then say "look at my board."

The reason for the two clipboard layers is worth saying plainly: modern vision models read a clean sketch almost perfectly well on their own. What they do badly is commit. Given only the picture they hedge (which line does that label belong to, is that word really what it looks like), and hedging in an agent workflow turns into either a clarifying question or a wrong build. The written layer removes the ambiguity rather than the illegibility.

This is the first release, so it is deliberately small: one canvas, one export, one tool for agents to call. Write-back, where the agent leaves sticky notes on your board, is the next thing.
